messages.author: 014d00e7482d028b
messages.subject: Changing scale on plot
parts:
Dear all,

I am making dynamic occupancy models for several species and I would like to plot the relationship of the different parameters (detection, colonization, etc) against some covariates.
I have manage to do this, but since I scaled my covariates before entering them in the models, now I have the X axis with the scaled scale (as is in the attached image).
Is there any straight forward code to adjust the plot to original covariate scale?
I know there are already some threds about this topic in the group, but I have not found a solution to my problem.
Any help and bit of code would be very helpfull.


Thank you.

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Changing scale on plot
parts:
Dear Pinto,

that's a classic. We ought to put the solution on some website ... Here's a sketch how to do this, based on some code I wrote just yesterday:

# Create prediction covariates on original scale in the range that you want (here, 200 - 3000 metres)
npred <- 100                                        
x.elev.orig <- seq(200, 3000, length.out = npred)

# Now transform the prediction covariate with mean and sd as computed from the actual covariate vector, which you used in scaled manner in the model fitting
x.elev <- ( x.elev.orig - mns[1] ) / sds[1]                  # This is like scale, but with custom mean and sd

# Then, use predict() on the fitted model object, and using x.elev as the covariate for which you predict

# Finally, to plot you can simply plot the prediction AGAINST THE ORIGINAL x.elev.orig and all is fine

Hope this makes sense ...

Best regards  -- Marc

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Changing scale on plot
parts:
Note that your mileage may vary with this suggestion:

Run the model without scaling/standardizing.  If you get (essentially) the same P-values for all parameters from the model with scaling, then that tells me that scaling wasn't necessary and getting predictions with the covariates in the original scale is then straightforward.  Scaling covariates is never wrong but its effects on increasing numerical precision (i.e., minimizing computer round-off error) doesn't always result in an improvement.

However, if there were "unscale = TRUE" and "scalingForAllCovariates = TRUE" options in those routines for model construction, predictions, and parameter tables, that would be really great.  I would certainly contribute (small amounts of) money and beverages of choice to those programming that.

Jim

messages.author: 4f80e1927b0757cb
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Changing scale on plot
parts:
You can use the scale() function inside your formulas.

Create the unmarked frame without standardizing any covariates. Then in your formula you can specify something like ~1~scale(elevation). The parameter estimates you see in the summary will be as if you standardized elevation beforehand. You can then just provide the covariate on the original scale in your newdata when using predict(), and it will be scaled automatically for you. See example below.

library(unmarked)

set.seed(1)
N <- 100
J <- 5
x <- rnorm(N, 2, 0.3)
psi <- plogis(-3 + 0.7*x)
z <- rbinom(N, 1, psi)
p <- 0.5

y <- matrix(NA, N, J)
for (i in 1:N){
  y[i,] <- rbinom(J, 1, p*z[i])
}

umf <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y, siteCovs=data.frame(x=x))

x_mn <- mean(x)
x_sd <- sd(x)

umf_scaled <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y, siteCovs=data.frame(x=(x-x_mn)/x_sd))

# Fit models (identical)
(mod_scaled <- occu(~1~x, umf_scaled))
(mod <- occu(~1~scale(x), umf))

# Make a range of x for plotting
range_x <- range(x)
new_x <- seq(range_x[1], range_x[2], length.out = 100)
# scale it manually
new_x_scaled <- (new_x - x_mn) / x_sd

nd <- data.frame(x = new_x)
nd_scaled <- data.frame(x = new_x_scaled)

pr_scaled <- predict(mod_scaled, 'state', newdata=nd_scaled)
pr <- predict(mod, 'state', newdata=nd)

head(pr_scaled)
head(pr)

plot(new_x, pr_scaled$Predicted, type='l')

plot(new_x, pr$Predicted, type='l')

On Thu, Apr 6, 2023 at 9:59 AM Ken Kellner <con...@kenkellner.com> wrote:
You can use the scale() function inside your formulas.

Create the unmarked frame without standardizing any covariates. Then in your formula you can specify something like ~1~scale(elevation). The parameter estimates you see in the summary will be as if you standardized elevation beforehand. You can then just provide the covariate on the original scale in your newdata when using predict(), and it will be scaled automatically for you. See example below.

library(unmarked)

set.seed(1)
N <- 100
J <- 5
x <- rnorm(N, 2, 0.3)
psi <- plogis(-3 + 0.7*x)
z <- rbinom(N, 1, psi)
p <- 0.5

y <- matrix(NA, N, J)
for (i in 1:N){
  y[i,] <- rbinom(J, 1, p*z[i])
}

umf <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y, siteCovs=data.frame(x=x))

x_mn <- mean(x)
x_sd <- sd(x)

umf_scaled <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y, siteCovs=data.frame(x=(x-x_mn)/x_sd))

# Fit models (identical)
(mod_scaled <- occu(~1~x, umf_scaled))
(mod <- occu(~1~scale(x), umf))

# Make a range of x for plotting
range_x <- range(x)
new_x <- seq(range_x[1], range_x[2], length.out = 100)
# scale it manually
new_x_scaled <- (new_x - x_mn) / x_sd

nd <- data.frame(x = new_x)
nd_scaled <- data.frame(x = new_x_scaled)

pr_scaled <- predict(mod_scaled, 'state', newdata=nd_scaled)
pr <- predict(mod, 'state', newdata=nd)

head(pr_scaled)
head(pr)

plot(new_x, pr_scaled$Predicted, type='l')

plot(new_x, pr$Predicted, type='l')

On Thursday, April 6, 2023 at 12:27:09 PM UTC-4 Jim Baldwin, USDA Forest Service wrote:
Note that your mileage may vary with this suggestion:

Run the model without scaling/standardizing.  If you get (essentially) the same P-values for all parameters from the model with scaling, then that tells me that scaling wasn't necessary and getting predictions with the covariates in the original scale is then straightforward.  Scaling covariates is never wrong but its effects on increasing numerical precision (i.e., minimizing computer round-off error) doesn't always result in an improvement.

However, if there were "unscale = TRUE" and "scalingForAllCovariates = TRUE" options in those routines for model construction, predictions, and parameter tables, that would be really great.  I would certainly contribute (small amounts of) money and beverages of choice to those programming that.

Jim

A quinta-feira, 6 de abril de 2023 à(s) 13:34:38 UTC+1, Kery Marc escreveu:
Dear Pinto,

that's a classic. We ought to put the solution on some website ... Here's a sketch how to do this, based on some code I wrote just yesterday:

# Create prediction covariates on original scale in the range that you want (here, 200 - 3000 metres)
npred <- 100                                        
x.elev.orig <- seq(200, 3000, length.out = npred)

# Now transform the prediction covariate with mean and sd as computed from the actual covariate vector, which you used in scaled manner in the model fitting
x.elev <- ( x.elev.orig - mns[1] ) / sds[1]                  # This is like scale, but with custom mean and sd

# Then, use predict() on the fitted model object, and using x.elev as the covariate for which you predict

# Finally, to plot you can simply plot the prediction AGAINST THE ORIGINAL x.elev.orig and all is fine

Hope this makes sense ...

Best regards  -- Marc

Hello there Sara,

yes I was able to build the plot. I ended up not using these plots but the code that worked for me was this:

# Predict colonization for the final model
final_pred_col <- predict(final_mod, type = 'col')
head(final_pred_col)

# Create covariate to have original scale values
npred <- 400  # 400 is the number of sites I have
x.lst.org <- as.data.frame(seq(22, 51, length.out = npred))
colnames(x.cov1.org) <- c("cov1")
head(x.cov1.org)

# Get data frame with range of scaled cov1 values
nd2_col <- data.frame(("cov1" = (seq(min(unmarkedMultFrame_ev@yearlySiteCovs$cov1), max(unmarkedMultFrame_ev@yearlySiteCovs$cov1), length.out=400))))
colnames(nd2_col) <- c("cov1")
head(nd2_col)

# Predict final model against scaled values
final_pred_col <- predict(final_mod, type = 'col', newdata= nd2_col)
print(predictions<-cbind( final_pred_col , x.cov1.org))
head(predictions)

# Plot predicted values against ORIGINAL cov1 values (not scaled)
plot(1, xlim=range(predictions$cov1), ylim=c(0,1), type="n", axes=T, xlab="Covariate 1",
pch=20, ylab="Colonization Probability",

cex.lab=1.25, cex.main=1.75)

lines(predictions$cov1, predictions$Predicted, col="blue", lwd=2)
lines(predictions$cov1, predictions$lower, lty=2, col="black")
lines(predictions$cov1, predictions$upper, lty=2, col="black")
